html:
Power Electronics & Protection
Intelligent MCC (iMCC) for Engineers: Architecture, Smart Relays, Protocols, IO Savings and Troubleshooting

An iMCC puts a smart motor management relay or drive in every feeder and sends all motor data to the DCS over one network. We will go through the architecture, the data you get, the cable savings and how to fix communication loss.

Smart relays Profibus and Profinet IO savings calculator Comms troubleshooting

An iMCC replaces hundreds of hardwired control signals with one industrial network and gives every feeder real diagnostics. We explain how it works, what it saves and how to keep it communicating.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn what an intelligent MCC is, how its smart feeders talk to the DCS and how to commission and troubleshoot one.
Quick Answer

What is an intelligent MCC and how is it different from a normal MCC?

Intelligent MCC means a normal low voltage motor control centre in which each feeder carries a smart motor management relay, VFD or soft starter connected to the DCS or PLC over Profibus, Profinet, Modbus TCP or EtherNet/IP. Instead of 7 hardwired signals per motor, one network drop carries start, stop, status, current and trip cause. For 40 motors that removes 280 IO points and 560 cores.

What Is an Intelligent MCC?

An intelligent MCC is a motor control centre whose starters, drives and meters are smart devices that measure, protect and report over an industrial network. So an intelligent MCC turns every motor feeder into a source of data on the network, for the DCS and for the maintenance team.

Key Facts
  • Eaton calls an MCC intelligent when it is integrated with communications and smart devices.
  • Typical devices are SIMOCODE pro, TeSys T, ABB UMC100.3, VFDs and soft starters.
  • Common networks are Profibus DP, Profinet, Modbus TCP and EtherNet/IP.
  • The power section still follows IEC 61439 2 and starters follow IEC 60947 4 1.

The power side is the same as in our guide on how a motor control center works. Busbars, withdrawable buckets, MCCB, contactor and form of separation stay unchanged, and only the control and protection layer becomes smart.

Do You Know?

Wikipedia notes that motor control centres have been used since 1950, first by the automobile industry. The intelligent MCC is the same idea with a communication layer added decades later.

Advertisement

How Does an Intelligent Motor Control Center Work?

A smart relay in each feeder does protection and logic locally, while it exchanges commands and measured data with the control system over a fieldbus or Ethernet. The DCS sends a start bit, the relay closes the contactor and sends back status, current and alarms within one bus cycle.

A conventional panel needs a run relay, a separate thermal overload relay, auxiliary feedback contacts and often a 4 to 20 mA current transducer. Each signal is a pair of cores running to marshalling and then to a DCS IO card.

1. CommandOperator presses start and the DCS writes a start bit
2. NetworkProfibus or Profinet carries the output bytes to the feeder
3. Relay logicThe relay checks interlocks and energises the contactor coil
4. MeasureBuilt in CTs measure 3 phase current and thermal capacity
5. FeedbackStatus, current and trip cause return to the DCS faceplate

Because protection lives inside the relay, the motor stays protected even when the network fails. Overload, phase failure and earth fault trips work without the DCS, and the network only adds control and visibility.

Intelligent MCC Architecture and Block Diagram

The intelligent MCC architecture has three layers: the control system, a network of switches or a Profibus master, and the smart feeders with their motors. Each feeder keeps its own short circuit device and contactor, and only the control path is shared.

Eaton recommends home run star wiring so that a lost link drops only one feeder, and notes that managed switches can also close a ring. The same choices are covered in our article on DCS network redundancy.

Siemens SIMOCODE pro

Modular system in pro S and pro V versions with current, voltage and thermistor modules.

Best for: Siemens DCS on Profibus or Profinet
Smart relay
Schneider TeSys T

LTMR controller with 6 inputs, 3 relay outputs and CTs for 0.4 to 100 A, or 810 A with external CTs.

Best for: Modbus, Profibus or EtherNet/IP plants
Smart relay
ABB UMC100.3

Universal motor controller for 0.24 to 63 A with trip classes 5, 10, 20, 30 and 40.

Best for: ABB 800xA systems and skids
Smart relay
VFD with comms card

Drive with a network option card giving speed, current and fault codes.

Best for: Pumps, fans and conveyors
Drive
Quick Tip

Keep the emergency stop and any SIL rated trip hardwired to the contactor coil or a safety relay. Let the network only report that the trip happened.

What Data Does a Smart Motor Management Relay Give?

A smart motor management relay gives the DCS motor status, 3 phase current, thermal capacity, trip cause, warnings, run hours and starts. Devices with a voltage module also add voltage, power factor and energy.

Data pointSourceHow you use it
Running, trippedStatus bitsFaceplate and interlocks
Phase currentsBuilt in CTsDry run and choke detection
Thermal capacity %Thermal modelWarn before an overload trip
Trip causeFault registerFault finding without opening the bucket
Run hours, startsCountersMaintenance and starts per hour limit
kW, kWh, PFVoltage moduleEnergy reports

Schneider lists thermal overload, phase reversal, phase imbalance, ground fault, PTC thermistor and stall detection among TeSys T functions. That overlaps with the motor protection relay types used on high voltage motors.

iMCC Communication Protocols: Profibus, Profinet, Modbus TCP and EtherNet/IP

The intelligent MCC network is usually Profibus DP or Profinet in Siemens plants, EtherNet/IP in Rockwell plants and Modbus TCP in mixed vendor plants. Pick the protocol your DCS supports natively, because every gateway adds a failure point.

ProtocolPhysical layerWatch out for
Profibus DPRS 485, up to 12 MbpsTermination, segment length
ProfinetEthernet, 100 MbpsDevice names, switch settings
EtherNet/IPEthernet, 100 MbpsEDS files, multicast load
Modbus TCPEthernet, 100 MbpsManual register map
Modbus RTURS 485 serialSlow polling with many slaves

The Siemens Smart MCC communications manual states that Profibus DP runs at up to 12 Mbps with 100 m per segment at that speed. It lists SIMOCODE pro V cyclic data of 10 input bytes and 4 output bytes in one telegram type, so even 40 motors need only a few hundred bytes per cycle.

Field Tip
Compare Profibus vs Profinet and Modbus RTU vs Modbus TCP before you freeze the intelligent MCC specification. Ask the vendor for GSD, GSDML or EDS files early so the DCS hardware configuration can start in parallel.

Smart MCC vs Conventional MCC

A smart MCC differs from a conventional MCC only in the control layer, where relays, auxiliary contacts and transducers become one networked device per feeder. The power circuit and short circuit rating stay the same.

FeatureConventional MCCIntelligent MCC
Control signals5 to 10 wired pairs per motorOne network drop per feeder
OverloadBimetal relayThermal model with warnings
DiagnosticsTripped lampTrip cause, current, counters
DCS IODI, DO, AI cardsOne comms module
SettingsDial in bucketRemote, password controlled
CostLower device costLower cabling cost
Advantages
  • Far fewer control cables, glands and terminals
  • Trip cause visible on the DCS
  • Thermal warning before a trip
  • Run hours support predictive maintenance
  • Less work near live parts
Limitations
  • Higher cost per feeder
  • Needs network and cybersecurity skills
  • One bad switch can blank many motors
  • Firmware and device files must be managed
Myth: An intelligent MCC stops protecting motors when the network fails.
Fact: Protection runs inside each relay, so overload and earth fault trips still work.
Myth: An iMCC only pays off in very large plants.
Fact: A 20 motor package already saves 140 points at 7 signals per motor.
Myth: The emergency stop can go on Profinet.
Fact: Standard Profinet is not a safety network, so use hardwired or certified safety channels.

How Many Hardwired IO Points Does an iMCC Save?

An intelligent MCC saves N × (DI + DO + AI) hardwired IO points, where N is the number of motors. Multiply the points by 2 for control cable cores, since each signal uses one pair.

Solved example: 40 motors
Points = N × (DI + DO + AI)
= 40 × (4 + 2 + 1) = 280 points
Cores = 2 × 280 = 560 cores
DI cards = 160 ÷ 16 = 10
DO cards = 80 ÷ 16 = 5
AI cards = 40 ÷ 8 = 5
Total = 20 IO cards

Here the 4 inputs are running, tripped, remote and available, the 2 outputs are start and stop, and the analog input is current. Check the DCS IO allocation sheet of a similar project before you fix your numbers.

Intelligent MCC IO Savings Calculator
Hardwired items replaced
280 IO points, 560 cores and about 20 IO cards replaced by 40 network drops

The calculator assumes 16 channel digital and 8 channel analog cards without spares. To check network load, use our network bandwidth calculator with the cyclic bytes from the device manual.

Do You Know?

A Control Engineering case study describes a retrofit with five new control panels supporting 434 motor starters. It states that intelligent motor management reduced discrete PLC IO, field wiring and installation work.

Intelligent MCC Selection and Commissioning Checklist

Select an intelligent MCC by matching the device and protocol to your DCS, then commission it in order: addressing, parameters, network test, loop check and live run. Skipping the network test before running motors causes most delays.

1
Freeze protocol
Confirm DCS interface, topology and redundancy before ordering.
2
Set motor data
Enter nameplate FLC, trip class and CT ratio for each feeder.
3
Address devices
Set Profibus addresses or Profinet names from one register.
4
Test network
Check terminators, shields and bus diagnostics with motors off.
5
Loop check
Verify start, stop, status and current from the DCS.
6
Run and back up
Compare running current with FLC and save parameters.
  • Device files match the firmware version
  • Emergency stop tested without the network
  • FLC and trip class match each nameplate
  • Parameter backups stored
  • Unused switch ports disabled

Take FLC from the nameplate as explained in our note on motor full load current. The site sequence mirrors our DCS commissioning steps article.

Troubleshooting Communication Loss in an Intelligent MCC

First check whether one feeder or all feeders are lost, because that shows whether the fault is at the device or at the switch, master or controller. Then check device LEDs, cable, termination and addressing in that order.

SymptomLikely causeFix
All feeders lostSwitch power or master cardCheck 24 V supply and link LEDs
One feeder lostLoose plug or damaged cableReseat plug, test cable
Random Profibus dropoutsWrong terminationTerminate both segment ends only
Lost after replacementAddress not setSet address or use init module
Current reads zeroWrong mapping or CT ratioCheck byte map and CT settings
Quick Tip

Siemens offers an initialization module that automatically configures a replacement SIMOCODE device. Fit one per bucket so a technician can swap a relay without a laptop.

For Modbus panels, our Modbus RTU troubleshooting guide covers polling, parity and address conflicts. An industrial protocol gateway links mixed vendors, but keep a spare because it is a single point of failure.

Feeders can be direct on line or star delta, and our DOL vs star delta comparison helps you choose. Drive feeders behave like any variable frequency drive with a comms card added.

This Eaton video shows an intelligent MCC being built and tested in the factory. Eaton says factory setting of IP addresses and protection values shortens site commissioning.

A relay that accepts a remote start can also accept a malicious one, so plan segmentation and passwords early. For more on networks, read our page on PLC communication protocols.

Intelligent MCC FAQ

What is an intelligent MCC and what does iMCC stand for?

An intelligent MCC, or iMCC, is a motor control centre where every feeder uses a smart relay, drive or meter on a network. It sends status, current, thermal capacity and trip cause to the DCS without hardwired signals.

Busbars and buckets stay the same.

What is the difference between conventional MCC and intelligent MCC with example?

A conventional MCC sends each motor signal over a wired pair, while an iMCC sends them all over one network drop. For 40 motors with 7 signals each, the conventional panel needs 280 IO points and 560 cores.

The smart panel needs 40 network drops.

How to calculate IO points saved by an intelligent motor control centre?

Multiply the number of motors by DI plus DO plus AI per motor. For 40 motors with 4 DI, 2 DO and 1 AI, the answer is 280 points.

Double the points to get cable cores, which gives 560 cores here.

Which communication protocol is best for an iMCC in process plants?

The best protocol is the one your DCS supports natively, usually Profibus DP or Profinet for Siemens and EtherNet/IP for Rockwell. Modbus TCP suits mixed vendor plants.

Avoid gateways where possible, because each one adds configuration work and a failure point.

Why does a single feeder lose communication in an intelligent MCC?

A single feeder usually drops because of a loose plug, damaged cable, wrong address or failed device. Check the device LED first, then cable and terminator.

If all feeders drop together, check the switch, its 24 V supply or the master card.

Does a smart motor relay still protect the motor if the network fails?

Yes, overload, phase failure and earth fault logic run inside the relay, so protection continues. You can also set most relays to stop or keep running on comms loss.

Choose that comms loss action for each motor based on the process risk.

What We Learn Today

  • An intelligent MCC keeps the normal power section but uses smart relays, drives and meters that report status, current and trip cause over a network.
  • The IO saving equals motors times signals per motor, so 40 motors with 7 signals each remove 280 points and 560 control cable cores.
  • Comms loss is found by checking whether one or all feeders dropped, then device LEDs, cables, terminators and addresses in that order.
